stem.text: Let \( f(x) = \frac{3}{- x - 3} \). The Taylor series for f about \( x = -4 \) is \( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 3 \left(\frac{x + 4}{1}\right)^{n} \). Its radius of convergence is \( 1 \). Does the series converge to f at \( x = -5 \)? Give a reason for the answer.

answer_key.label: No, because \( x = -5 \) is an endpoint that the interval of convergence \( -5 < x < -3 \) excludes.

worked_solution.text: The ratio test gives convergence for \( \left|x + 4\right| < 1 \), the interior \( -5 < x < -3 \), and \( x = -5 \) is an endpoint.
At \( x = -5 \) the series is \( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 3 (-1)^{n} \), whose terms do not approach 0, so it diverges there. The interval of convergence is \( -5 < x < -3 \).

options.label: Yes, because \( x = -5 \) lies in the interval of convergence \( -5 \le x < -3 \).
options.derivation: the excluded left endpoint written into the interval with a closed bracket

options.derivation: the geometric sum formula applied with ratio -1, whose size is not less than 1
